lorebooks.name: Unregistered - the valley of the Lyrasil

entries.name: Setting
entries.payload: The Lyrasil valley (the Ledger calls it Zint-karn, the tax-land; the river Vat-veg, the water-road; the town Zorg-ort, the provisions-place), a river province of the Vrakht Dominion, an empire of iron and ledgers that conquered it eleven years ago. Fort Stein-krog holds the garrison above the river town of Silvakhor; the Lyrshara, the people of the valley, farm the flood meadows and fish the reeds. The Dominion rules by record: every person belongs to a line of the Ledger, and a person with no line pays the life-tax, the liv-zint, with years of work. The world has one sun, one moon, no machines beyond water mills and clockwork scales, and a few hexe, hedge-witches the Dominion tolerates and distrusts. The Lyrshara speak Aethel-Vael, the whispering tongue, among themselves and use Vrakht with the Dominion. Prague appears only in the first parts, and as a memory.

entries.name: Style
entries.payload:
Third person, past tense, close to the point of view character. Show feelings through gesture and speech. Several paragraphs per part, no summary of what comes next, end on a moment the next part can pick up. No headings.

LANGUAGES. Write ALL speech in plain English inside the quotation marks, whatever language the character speaks, and name the language in the narration ONLY WHEN IT CHANGES: the first line of a conversation in a language other than English, and again only when the speaker switches to another language. English is the language of the book, so a line in English needs no cue unless it comes straight after a line in another language. The lines that follow in the same language need no cue at all; the reader knows who is talking to whom. Examples: "she said in Japanese", "he muttered in Czech", "in Vrakht", "in Aethel-Vael", "in broken English". Never write "he said in English" as a habit. A translator turns the English into that language AFTER you; you never do. So NEVER write words or phrases of Japanese, Czech, Vrakht or Aethel-Vael yourself: no romaji, no kana, no other script, no transliteration, no italic translation after a foreign phrase, no gloss, no honorific suffixes such as -san. The only foreign words allowed are the names of people and places. When the point of view character does not understand the language, the narration says so and gives tone, gestures and sounds, never the meaning in the character's head; the quoted English is still what was said. Broken English is written as broken English. A character's THOUGHTS are always written in English, the language of the book, never in the language the character would think in. Muttering, whispering and speaking under one's breath are speech: put them in quotation marks like the rest.
entries.comment: Always active; right before the instructions of the part. The line about quoted English is what the translators rely on.

entries.name: Tomáš Hájek
entries.payload: **Tomáš Hájek** - twenty-nine, Czech, guide in the Prague underground tours. Tall, untidy, a headlamp always on his forehead. Fluent English from the tours; his Japanese comes from novels, subtitles and four years of self-study, so it is stiff, bookish and sometimes anime-sounding (wrong politeness at the wrong time). Mutters in Czech when he is stressed. Keeps a paper notebook of words. Hid his Japanese because it embarrasses him; likes to explain things; secretly does not want to go home.

entries.name: Mizuki Hayashida
entries.payload: **Mizuki Hayashida** - twenty-seven, Japanese, a nurse from Sendai on her first trip abroad. Small, practical, watches before she speaks. School English only, so she speaks broken English to strangers. Mutters in Japanese when she is alone or thinks no one understands. Has a younger brother she calls every Sunday. Touches the wound first, asks questions after.

entries.name: Saellen
entries.payload: **Saellen** - forty-four, Lyrshara, the ferrywoman of Silvakhor landing. Broad, weather-brown, sings under her breath. Speaks Aethel-Vael at home and market Vrakht to the soldiers; loses patience with fools and never with the hungry.

entries.name: Steing
entries.payload: **Steing** - fifty-one, Vrakht, life-tax assessor of the Lyrasil valley. Thin, ink to the elbows, a mouth that tightens before he says no. Believes in the Ledger as other men believe in gods. Uses Hoh, the patronizing tone, even on his friends, and has a secret that his columns hide.

entries.name: Aelmoria
entries.payload: **Aelmoria** - sixty-eight, Lyrshara, the reed-mother, the hedge-witch of Kaelthal. Calls herself a herbwife; the Dominion calls her a hexe. Small, bent, very still, sharp eyes. Knows that the valley has a door that opens at low water on the new moon, and has waited a long time for someone to come through it.

entries.name: Paskal
entries.payload: **Paskal** - nineteen, Vrakht conscript from the far steppe, homesick, strong, cheerful, bad at hiding that he is afraid. Teaches Tomáš army words as a game; the first person in the fort to treat the two as people.

entries.name: Mangel
entries.payload: **Lieutenant Mangel** - twenty-five, Vrakht officer of Fort Stein-krog. Straight-backed, ambitious, honest in a way that hurts her career. Speaks Gna to her commander and Bef to everyone else; wants the valley quiet and her name in a good report.

entries.name: Frecht
entries.payload: **Commander Frecht** - fifty-eight, commander of Fort Stein-krog. Tired, fat, clever, wants nothing to change before his pension.

entries.name: Inspector Kestim
entries.payload: **Inspector Kestim** - forty-seven, Vrakht, auditor of the capital. Dry, polite, never raises her voice, reads a ledger like a face. Arrives after the autumn count.

entries.name: Reed Fields
entries.payload: **The reed fields** - the flood meadow of the Lyrasil above Silvakhor landing: head-high reeds, black water, mud, a huge low moon. Where the two wake.

entries.name: Ferry Landing
entries.payload: **Silvakhor landing** - a flat ferry on a rope across the Lyrasil, a lantern on a pole, Saellen's hut beside the slip.

entries.name: Silvakhor
entries.payload: **Silvakhor** - the Lyrshara river town: timber houses on stilts, a market square, a stone chapel with a deep granary under it, the weir and its mill. Lyrshara homes are low and quiet; the Dominion posts a soldier at each end of the bridge.

entries.name: Fort Stein-krog
entries.payload: **Fort Stein-krog** - the garrison on the hill above Silvakhor: grey walls, a drill yard, the barracks, the infirmary, the store rooms, and the Ledger House where Steing keeps the books. Smells of iron, wet wool and lamp oil.

entries.name: Ledger House
entries.payload: **The Ledger House** - a long cold room in the fort with slanted desks, brass counting frames and shelves of the Ledger, bound by year. A person exists here when a line says so.

entries.name: Kaelthal
entries.payload: **Kaelthal** - a wooded dip an hour's walk from Silvakhor; Aelmoria's hut, drying herbs, a spring and an old standing stone at the edge of the reeds.

entries.name: The Weir
entries.payload: **The weir of Silvakhor** - an old timber-and-stone dam that holds back the Lyrasil above the mill; in autumn rain it is the town's one danger.

entries.name: Prague Cellar
entries.payload: **The Prague cellar** - a Gothic basement of the Old Town, a tourist tour that closes at nine; one wall holds a bricked archway the tour never mentions.

entries.name: The Dominion
entries.payload: **The Vrakht Dominion** - an empire of garrisons, roads and records. Soldiers and clerks call everyone by rank and line; gold is counted, years are taxed. Its army is built from conscripts of the steppe. The Dominion language, Vrakht, is the language of orders.

entries.name: The Lyrshara
entries.payload: **The Lyrshara** (the Dominion calls them skag-folk, the enemy-people, which they know and do not use) - the valley people: river folk, slow to anger, long memories. Their own language is Aethel-Vael, soft and fluid (the story says "in Aethel-Vael" or "in their own tongue"), spoken among themselves and quoted as English like any speech; they use market Vrakht with the occupiers, and slip into Aethel-Vael when they do not want to be understood. Many hide grain from the tithe.

entries.name: The Ledger
entries.payload: **The Ledger** - the Dominion's book of persons. A line has a name, a stamm (house/line), a guarantor and a tax. A person with no line has nobody to answer for them and owes the life-tax.

entries.name: Life-tax
entries.payload: **The life-tax (liv-zint)** - a debt measured in years of work, assessed on a person without a line; commuted if a guarantor of the Ledger signs for them and the person has a trade. The assessor gives a person ninety days to be entered.

entries.name: Tally token
entries.payload: **The tally token** - a stamped tin disc with the number of a person's provisional line, worn on a cord. Without it a person can be stopped by any soldier.

entries.name: Tomáš's notebook
entries.payload: **Tomáš's notebook** - a small black paper notebook; his Japanese vocabulary and now his Vrakht lists, written in Czech, Japanese and Latin letters at once. Nobody else can read it.

entries.name: Phone and watch
entries.payload: **The phones and the headlamp** - Mizuki's phone is dead from the start (its battery was empty before the cellar). Tomáš's phone works at first (58 percent, no signal) and dies after the second day. His headlamp is cracked and dim, but it still works: in the fort the soldiers call its light 'hexe-werk' and take it, and Steing logs the things as goods.

entries.name: Tone prefixes
entries.payload: **Vrakht tone prefixes** - a sentence begins with a mood (Da statement, Frag question, Bef command) and often a tone: Gna polite, Hoh patronizing, Droh threatening, Acht urgent, Mok mocking, Fall resigned. A Vrakht speaker's attitude is audible before the first word is understood.

entries.name: Reed-door
entries.payload: **The reed-door** - a place at the edge of Kaelthal where, at low water on the new moon, the reeds part on a lit archway. It opens rarely; whoever steps through goes where it leads. Only the reed-mothers know.

entries.name: Japanese between them
entries.payload: Tomáš and Mizuki talk Japanese when alone: his is stiff and over-polite or accidentally boyish, hers is natural and a little teasing; they slip into English only for a word one lacks. Nobody else in the world understands it; the soldiers think it is a chant.

entries.name: Isekai tropes
entries.payload: Tomáš knows the genre from novels and jokes about it (status windows, a summoner, a cheat ability). The world offers none of these. Mizuki finds it tiresome and then, slowly, useful.

entries.name: Draft: the capital
entries.payload: Karhold, the capital, a stone city of nine rings. NOT USED in this story; kept as a draft.
